newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Cairns Group set to blast EU on farm subsidies.
newsitem.headline: Cairns Group set to blast EU on farm subsidies.

text.p: The Cairns Group of farm exporting countries will slam the European Union on Friday for what it regards as gross violations of trading agreements in the EU's support for farm subsidies, Philippine Trade and Industry Secretary Cesar Bautista said.

Wrangling between the EU on one hand and the U.S. and the Cairns Group, linking farm exporting nations from Australia to Uruguay, on the other was only settled after the dropping of a paragraph proposed by Argentina to mandate preliminary studies on farm issues in 1997 in a statement to be issued at the World Trade Organisation (WTO) meeting here.
"The solution to that is for the Cairns Group to issue a separate statement (on farm trade)," Bautista told reporters in a news conference.

He said the Cairns Group planned to issue its statement criticising the EU stance after seeing the wording of the reference to agriculture in the WTO's final declaration to be issued later on Friday at the end of the WTO ministerial conference.

"The gist of that statement is to really deplore the non-compliance of the Uruguay Round agreements on export subsidies and domestic support," he said. "The EU is the biggest violator of agricultural subsidies."

Bautista said Argentina's proposal to insert language to initiate discussions on farm issues in 1997 was dropped because of dogged objections by EU officials who said the statement was unnecessary since formal talks on farm trade will begin anyway in 1999.
The revised farm statement in the WTO declaration will take note of problems in agricultural trade, but will not specifically single out the EU over the issue of farm subsidies, Bautista added.
Liberalising farm trade was one of the most contentious issues in the last round of global trade talks, the Uruguay Round, which ended in 1994.
An Asian official said the Argentine proposal was deleted to ensure that the WTO's final declaration would include something on agriculture.
"I would be bitterly disappointed if agriculture did not make it into the conference declaration," Australian Deputy Prime Minister Tim Fischer told a news conference on Thursday.
Fischer said he believes progress will eventually be made on liberalising farm trade.

The Cairns Group and the United States are campaigning hard to free up farm trade, and both have endorsed the faster elimination of agricultural barriers. The EU, along with Japan and South Korea, are reluctant to do so.
